titre: Stradivarius vs. New Violins: The 2014 Blind Test in Paris
accroche: Ten soloists played twelve violins behind welder's goggles: six chose a new violin to replace their own
contenu_vulgarise:
In a rehearsal room in a house in the Paris suburbs, the lights are dimmed and the soloists wear modified welder's goggles. They play violins they cannot see, while researchers record their judgments. Among the twelve instruments, five are Stradivarius.

## The protocol

The study appears in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* in 2014. It is signed by Claudia Fritz, Joseph Curtin, Jacques Poitevineau, Palmer Morrel-Samuels, and Fan-Chia Tao. Ten internationally renowned soloists, or winners of major competitions, take part. They test six old Italian violins, five of them by Stradivari, and six new violins, built by professional luthiers from Europe and North America, antiqued to look old, aged from a few days to twenty years.

Each soloist has two 75-minute sessions: one in the rehearsal room, the other in a 300-seat concert hall. He or she plays with their own bow. The goggles and the reduced light prevent identifying the instrument by sight, and the antiquing of the new violins removes cues by touch. A smell could have betrayed the age of the varnish: the authors proposed masking it, the owners of the old violins refused, for fear for the varnish, and no one reported a distinctive smell.

## What the soloists decided

Six soloists out of ten choose a new violin to replace their own on a hypothetical tour. Four choose an old violin: the authors write that they choose Stradivarius. A single new violin, rated N5, is the most appreciated of the twelve: it collects 26 points in the hall, against 13 for the next one. Adding up the preference points, the new violins total 35 and the old ones 4. For playability, articulation, and projection, the best new violins are rated higher than the best old ones, and at least equal for timbre.

When asked to say whether a violin is old or new, the soloists are wrong about half the time. The authors also point out an inconsistency in their own article: the text counts 31 right answers and 33 wrong ones, the table the reverse. In both cases, it is at chance level.

## What the test does not say

The ten soloists do not form a random sample: the authors stick to descriptive statistics. Twelve violins is few, and six old Italian ones do not represent all Stradivarius. Four soloists, in fact, preferred a Stradivarius for their tour: the study does not say that these instruments sound bad.

It shifts the question. The received idea is that a soloist immediately hears what distinguishes an 18th-century instrument from a contemporary violin. Here, deprived of sight, the soloists do not find this difference by ear, and their preferences go more often to the new violins.

In this study, only the soloists judge: what a listener in the twentieth row hears is not measured in it.

repere.texte: Ten soloists, twelve violins, two 75-minute sessions: six soloists out of ten choose a new violin to replace their own, and the most appreciated violin in the hall is a new one, with 26 points against 13 for the next one.
repere.source: Fritz et al., “Soloist evaluations of six Old Italian and six new violins,” PNAS 111(20), 2014

carte.punch: Six soloists out of ten chose a new violin for their tour, without seeing the instrument.
carte.idee: In 2014, ten soloists played twelve violins behind welder's goggles, five of them Stradivarius. Six chose a new violin to replace their own, and their answers when guessing an instrument's age did not exceed chance.

quiz.question: Why were the study's new violins antiqued to look old?
choix: So that their sound would come closer to that of the old violins before the trials
To remove cues by touch, such as unworn edges, that betray age
So that the owners of the old violins would agree to lend their instruments
So that the soloists would recognize the new violins faster during the trials
quiz.explication: The antiquing removes age cues by touch, such as unworn edges, in the same way that the goggles and reduced light remove visual cues. It does not change the sound, was not a condition set by the owners, and it aimed to prevent recognition, not to make it easier.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What score did the new violin N5, the most appreciated in the rehearsal room, obtain, compared with the second-best-rated violin?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that N5 gets 26 preference points in the rehearsal room, against 13 for the next violin, double; the other figures match no score cited in the entry.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When soloists are asked to say whether the violin they have just played is old or new, how often are they wrong?
choix: About half the time, which is chance level
Less than one time in ten, the soloists' ear almost always spots the age
Nearly three times out of four, they systematically confuse new and old
Never, they correctly identify every violin in both sessions
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text notes about one right answer in two, which matches pure chance; the authors even point out an inconsistency between the text and the table on this figure, but both versions remain close to chance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was the smell of the varnish not masked during the trials, when it could have betrayed a violin's age?
choix: Because the researchers judged the measure useless, no soloist having a keen enough sense of smell
Because the welder's goggles already sufficed to mask any distinctive smell
Because the 300-seat concert hall ventilated too fast for a smell to linger
Because the owners of the old violins refused, for fear for the varnish
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The authors proposed masking the smell, but the owners of the old violins refused for fear for the varnish; the text specifies that no one afterward reported a distinctive smell during the trials.
